overview:
Korea had been a Japanese colony for thirty-five years when the empire collapsed in 1945, and the peninsula was divided almost casually — American and Soviet officers agreeing on the 38th parallel as a line for accepting the Japanese surrender. What began as an administrative convenience hardened into two rival states by 1948, each claiming the whole country, and the border was already bleeding from guerrilla campaigns and cross-parallel raids before any formal war. Documents that emerged from Soviet and Chinese archives after 1991 show Kim Il Sung pressing Stalin repeatedly for permission to invade, being refused in 1949, and winning conditional approval in 1950 once Stalin judged the Americans unlikely to fight and required that Mao also consent. The invasion came on 25 June 1950. With the Soviet delegate boycotting the Security Council, the United Nations authorized a military response, and a war between Koreans became a war involving twenty-odd nations.

The fighting swung the length of the peninsula twice in nine months. South Korean and hastily committed American units were shattered at Osan and Taejon and driven into a shrinking box around Pusan, where they held through August. MacArthur's amphibious landing at Inchon in September cut the North Korean army's supply line and collapsed it; UN forces crossed the parallel and pushed toward the Yalu, at which point Chinese "volunteers" entered in force, mauling the Eighth Army along the Ch'ongch'on River and mangling the Marines at the frozen Changjin (Chosin) Reservoir. Seoul changed hands four times. By mid-1951 the front had ground to a halt near where the war started, and the remaining two years were fought over named hills — Heartbreak Ridge, Pork Chop Hill — while armistice talks dragged through 158 meetings at Kaesong and Panmunjom, deadlocked mainly over whether prisoners who refused to go home could be forced to. Behind the static front, American air power dropped more tonnage on Korea than on the entire Pacific theatre of the Second World War, leaving most North Korean towns in ruins.

The armistice signed on 27 July 1953 was a military document, not a peace, and no treaty has replaced it; the four-kilometre demilitarized zone it created is still there. Estimates of the dead run from roughly two and a half to three million, and more than half were civilians — a proportion higher than in either the Second World War or Vietnam. Much of that killing was not battlefield killing. South Korean authorities executed perhaps a hundred thousand or more detainees of the Bodo League in the war's first weeks; retreating and advancing forces on both sides settled scores in villages; American units killed refugees they feared were infiltrators, as at No Gun Ri. The Sinchon killings of late 1950, which North Korea presents in a dedicated museum as an American atrocity of some thirty-five thousand dead, are attributed by South Korean investigators and most outside historians to right-wing security police and vigilantes amid reciprocal local slaughter — a dispute that stands for how much of this war's civilian record remains contested.
significance: This was the first shooting war of the Cold War, and it set the terms for the four decades that followed: great powers fighting each other through proxies and deniable "volunteers", deliberately kept limited beneath the nuclear threshold, and ended without victory. It converted American containment from a doctrine on paper into a permanent global military establishment, tripling defence spending, putting troops in Europe indefinitely, rearming Japan's economy through war procurement, and locking in the alliances with Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei that still structure East Asian security. For China it was a costly debut as a power willing to fight the United States to a standstill; for Korea it fixed a temporary line as a national wound that has now lasted longer than the unified country most of its victims remembered. The armistice remains unreplaced, which means the peninsula's soldiers face each other under a ceasefire signed in 1953.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, the US National Archives page on the armistice, the Wilson Center's description of its declassified Soviet, Chinese and North Korean document collections, and reference material on the Sinchon killings. The 69 events here are overwhelmingly battles, and overwhelmingly from 1950 — the mobile first year is well covered while the static 1951–53 fighting, the two years of negotiation, the air campaign, and the civilian catastrophe are barely represented. That skew mirrors the wider record: UN and American operational history is documented in detail, North Korean and Chinese sources remain partial and state-controlled, and casualty totals, massacre attributions and the scale of civilian killing are estimates rather than counts, several of them still actively disputed.
